control: A designated receipt station with a non-porous, bunded work surface and a leak-containment tray, so a leaking container is opened inside something.
A Class II biological safety cabinet available in the receiving area, with a written trigger for moving a visibly leaking or damaged container into it before opening.
Local exhaust or a dedicated room for opening containers flagged as high-risk respiratory specimens.
Any container found leaking, cracked or with visible external contamination is transferred unopened to a Class II cabinet.

The cabinet serving receipt is field-certified on the same schedule, and to the same recognised standard, as the cabinets serving microbiology. The laboratory records which standard and which interval it applies; this reference does not restate them.
Gloves and a fluid-resistant laboratory coat, as a minimum, for all container handling.
Eye and face protection when opening any container with external contamination or evidence of leakage.
Respiratory protection is not indicated for routine receipt and is indicated only for the leakage and breakage mode, under the laboratory's respiratory protection programme.
A written leaking-specimen procedure posted at the receipt station, not filed in a manual.
Rejection criteria that allow staff to refuse a container rather than open it.
A spill kit within reach of the receipt station, with a documented monthly check.
Immediate reporting of every breakage event, whether or not anyone was exposed.
Sealed safety buckets or a sealed rotor, loaded and unloaded inside a Class II biological safety cabinet whenever the specimen may contain an inhalational hazard.
Centrifuges with a lid interlock that cannot be opened while the rotor turns.
Centrifuge sited away from walkways and from the operator's seated breathing zone.
For any specimen under profile P3, or any specimen flagged for mycobacterial or fungal culture, sealed buckets are opened only inside a certified Class II cabinet.
Gloves and fluid-resistant coat. Eye protection when unloading.
Respiratory protection is not recommended as a routine control for this step.

A written wait interval after the run before the lid is opened, and a second interval before sealed buckets are opened, so that any generated aerosol has time to settle. The reference deliberately specifies no number: no interval in the located evidence is derived from measurement of a clinical centrifuge, and a figure invented here would acquire false authority. The laboratory sets, records and justifies its own intervals.
Documented inspection of rotors, buckets, gaskets and O-rings on a defined schedule, with records retained.
Tube fill limits and a rule against centrifuging cracked, chipped or visibly damaged tubes.
A written breakage-in-the-centrifuge procedure, including who is told and when the room is re-entered.
Closed-tube sampling wherever the analyser supports it, which removes the step rather than controlling it.
Automated decapping enclosed within the instrument, in preference to manual decapping at the bench.
Where manual decapping is unavoidable for specimens under profile P2 or P3, it is done inside a Class II cabinet.
A splash shield at the decapping position does not control inhalation and is credited only against splash.
All manual opening of specimens flagged for mycobacterial, fungal or systemic bacterial culture occurs inside a certified Class II cabinet.
Gloves, fluid-resistant coat, and eye and face protection as the minimum for manual decapping.
A taught technique: tube held away from the face, stopper covered with absorbent gauze, twisted and lifted rather than pulled or rolled free.
A rule that tubes are allowed to come to rest after centrifugation before being opened.
Competency assessment on decapping technique at induction and on a defined interval, recorded.

control: Until this row is supported by measurement, the laboratory records that it is operating on precaution rather than evidence. That record is itself an ISO 35001 output.
The closed cartridge is the primary control and is already present. The reference's recommendation is to protect it, not to add to it.
Specimen and reagent mixing, and transfer into the cartridge, performed inside a Class II cabinet where the laboratory has one.
Instrument sited so that module doors do not open into a seated breathing zone.

Where a cabinet is available, all open transfer occurs within it. Where a cabinet is not available, the measured evidence supports benchtop loading provided the specified sample reagent contact time is honoured in full. The reference states this deliberately, because withholding it would push laboratories without a cabinet toward doing the step with no guidance at all.
Gloves and a fluid-resistant coat for all cartridge work.
Eye and face protection for the open transfer.
Respiratory protection where the laboratory's own risk assessment calls for it, under a documented programme.

Sample reagent used exactly as the manufacturer specifies: the correct reagent to sputum ratio, the correct dispensing method, and the full contact time. The reference does not single out one of the three, because the source read for this release does not establish which carries the inactivation.
The reagent step prompted and recorded at the bench rather than left to memory, since all three of its parameters are set by the operator.
A rule that a cartridge dropped or shaken after loading is discarded rather than run.
Used cartridges handled as infectious waste and never opened.
Competency assessment that specifically tests the reagent contact step.
All colony picking, broth transfer and target spotting performed inside a certified Class II biological safety cabinet, with only the sealed or inactivated target plate leaving it.
An inactivation or extraction step, rather than direct smear, for any isolate that has not been ruled out as a biological threat agent.
Target plates transported to the instrument in a closed carrier.
Cabinet use is the central recommendation for this step, and it is the one most often absent in practice.
The cabinet is field-certified on a defined schedule with records retained, and is not treated as a shelf when not in use.
Gloves and a fluid-resistant coat. Eye and face protection outside the cabinet.
For an isolate that cannot be ruled out under the sentinel protocols, the enhanced practices those protocols specify.

A standing rule that ANY slow-growing blood culture isolate is handled in a cabinet and entered into the rule-out algorithm, irrespective of its Gram stain appearance. This control is deliberately blind to the stain: in three of the four documented events involving this technology the stain appeared as Gram-positive rods or cocci suggesting streptococci, so a stain-triggered rule would not have fired.

A clinical and travel history cue available at the bench, so that an isolate from a patient with a compatible exposure history is escalated even when its laboratory appearance is unremarkable. This is the trigger the investigators themselves recommend, and it does not depend on the organism looking unusual.
A prompt tied to specimen type and growth rate rather than to morphology, placed in middleware or on the worksheet, firing before the isolate reaches the target plate.
An exposure assessment and notification procedure that can be run retrospectively on a work list, because recognition in this step is usually retrospective.
Referral to the Laboratory Response Network reference laboratory per the sentinel protocols rather than in-house identification.
A certified Class II biological safety cabinet for all manipulation of sterile-site isolates and all work on an organism that has not been ruled out.
Disposable loops and a closed electric incinerator in place of an open flame, so that no step requires flaming wet material.
Bench layout that puts the cabinet where the work naturally happens, rather than across the room from the plate reading bench.
Cabinet use is the single highest-value control in this reference, carried by the strongest evidence in it.

Field certification to a recognised standard on a defined schedule, with records retained, and re-certification after any relocation. The laboratory records which standard and which interval it applies.
No storage on the work surface, grilles kept clear, and a documented airflow check before use.
Gloves and a fluid-resistant coat inside the cabinet.
Where the sentinel protocols call for enhanced practices on a non-excluded isolate, the respiratory and face protection those protocols specify, under a documented programme.
A standing prohibition on smelling plates, written down rather than assumed.
A rule that slides are fully air dried before any heat is applied.
Immunisation offered and recorded for staff who routinely manipulate isolates for which an effective vaccine exists, as part of the worker health programme.
A documented exposure response pathway with named contacts and a defined prophylaxis window, rehearsed rather than filed.
Competency assessment on cabinet technique, not only on cabinet awareness.
